scenario_constructions: Priya Anand and Solano Bay Community Power are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case, Dana Okafor / the-turbine-channel, and Renata Alvarez / wind-call.

The specific capacity-contract decision, the board vote timeline, and the two-minute countdown in the Overview are fictional scenario details built around real CAISO demand data and real Lazard cost figures -- the numbers driving every downstream calculation are real and sourced; the specific contracts and decision moment are not.
MA1 (3% CAISO share) and MA2 ($10,000/month budget) are both stated scenario assumptions with no real citable source for this fictional district -- see Appendix E.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Solano Bay Community Power's share of CAISO's total system demand
modeling_assumptions.basis: Real California CCAs vary enormously in size (S4) and no single real published figure exists for this fictional district. 3% is a stated, mid-range illustrative share.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales every downstream MW/MWh figure (Challenges D3-D5) proportionally and does not change which contract wins the dollar-per-megawatt-hour comparison, since that ratio is scale-independent. It does change the absolute size of the capacity gap and total dollar costs shown in D3/D5.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The board's authorized monthly budget for this capacity tranche
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public figure exists for a fictional district's internal budget authorization; stated specifically to give Challenge D4's equation-solving work a real number to solve for.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Affects only Challenge D4's illustrative side-calculation (how much firming capacity the monthly budget alone could support). Does not affect either contract's dollar-per-megawatt-hour rate or the Dilemma's own balance.

sensitivity_note: SPEC Section 6 does not apply -- this is a capacity-procurement business decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: The Peaker Contract is fully dispatchable at 100% reliability with no additional accreditation charge of any kind -- a natural-gas peaking plant does not need a separate capacity-accreditation payment the way an intermittent resource does, and even at the real published low end of Lazard's national range, its $149 per megawatt-hour rate reflects a mature, well-understood technology with none of the newer capacity-accreditation-methodology uncertainty CAISO and other grid operators are still actively revising for solar-plus-storage (Appendix D itself notes CAISO has been actively lowering its own ELCC values for exactly this technology).
balance.argument_b: The Firmed Solar Contract wins on this case's own real, published numbers once both options are priced on the same 100%-firm basis: $142 per megawatt-hour (its own $73/MWh cost plus the real, CAISO-specific $69/MWh firming charge) against the Peaker Contract's $149 per megawatt-hour -- even using the most favorable realistic point in gas peaking's own real cost range. The gap is real but genuinely thin: about $7 per megawatt-hour, roughly 4.7% of the Peaker Contract's own rate.
balance.margin_basis: margin_pct = |149 - 142| / max(149, 142) x 100 = 4.70%. Both rates are Lazard's own real, published figures (S2, S3); no case-specific derivation changes either headline number. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.

deliverables.text: A descriptive-statistics table for the full 24-hour demand record (after filling in the missing hour in D2): median, first and third quartiles, range, and a stated, shown-work conclusion on whether the data set contains a statistical outlier.
A missing-data reconstruction, showing algebra: use the daily logged average and the 23 known hourly readings to find the redacted hour's demand, then verify by recomputing the full 24-hour mean.

A peak-window and capacity-sizing table: the hours Solano Bay's demand exceeds its third quartile, the district's own peak and third-quartile demand (scaled from CAISO's real figures), and the resulting new capacity in megawatts needed.

A unit-conversion and equation worksheet: convert the real firming charge from dollars per kilowatt-month into dollars per megawatt-year, then set up and solve a multi-step equation for the megawatts of firming capacity the monthly board budget could support.

A total-cost comparison table: for each contract, the megawatt-hours of coverage needed, the real dollar-per-megawatt-hour rate, and the resulting total dollar cost, with both rates stated side by side.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: case.json.balance.a_rate_usd_per_mwh (149) is the real, cited LOW END of Lazard's own published national gas-peaking LCOE range ($149-$251/MWh, S2), not the range's midpoint or high end -- disclosed explicitly in Appendix C and here rather than buried. This is a real, defensible modeling choice (Lazard's own methodology states the range reflects site-specific factors), but it is also the single most load-bearing choice in this case's balance: sensitivity_model.py's own PARAMS/FLEX do not sweep this value (it is cited data, not a stated scenario assumption, per Tier 2 probe 5's FLEX-scoping rule), but a Hero should be told plainly that using the range's midpoint (~$200/MWh) instead of its low end would widen Option B's margin well past this case's own 4.7%, while using the range's own higher points would eventually flip the recommendation to Option A. This is disclosed here in full, not softened.

This case's real-world setting (capacity-market firming economics, ELCC/Net CONE mechanics) is genuinely dense financial/regulatory machinery that a K-12 case cannot fully de-jargon without becoming a different case about energy-market design rather than the math it's built to teach — the same class of finding as this project's own carpenter/codebreaker P7 precedent. remaining_gaps: California ISO (CAISO) -- what it actually does day to day, how it "designates" plants
Resource adequacy planner -- the job function itself
Effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) -- the definition given a bit, but not how a percentage is actually computed from "historical performance"
Net cost of new entry ("Net CONE") -- why this specific dollar figure is the "cost of new entry" and how it's set
$/kW-month vs $/MWh vs $/MW-year -- no intuitive feel for these units relative to each other
Nameplate capacity vs regional capacity factor -- the distinction between a plant's rated size and how much it actually produces
Levelized cost of energy (LCOE) -- the "lifetime cost divided by lifetime output" idea is stated, but not how it's actually calculated in practice
Board packet / pre-board call -- organizational/procedural terms

MCS-51: the firming charge/backstop arrangement's own contractual trigger mechanics (who calls whom, how the trigger moment is detected) remain an administrative abstraction to a zero-context reader even after the added 3-step explanation and insurance analogy -- though the same round's reader called that analogy 'the clearest handhold offered.'
